whyThisMatters: Most breaches do not start with hacking. They start with someone opening the wrong email. Today you will build the habit of noticing.
rememberThis: Slow down for ten seconds before you click. That is usually all it takes to catch it.

discussionPrompts: Ask which detail people noticed first. Was it the sender address, the urgent wording, or the attachment? Would they check the same thing on their own phone?
For the link card for offshore crew, ask how many people actually hover over or press and hold a link before they tap it. What makes that hard to do with limited internet at sea?
Ask if anyone has seen a scam text or a fake IT pop-up like these in real life. What did they do?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often miss the fake domain and the fake portal. Both the real and fake images look almost the same. So people judge by which one looks more neat and professional. They do not check the exact address letter by letter.

items.title: Real vs Fake Offer Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake HR email comes from hr@synergymarine-group-careers.com. This adds an extra hyphen and the word "-careers". The real address is hr@synergymarinegroup.com. The subject and message look almost the same. Only the sender address is different.
items.whyItsSuspicious: HR teams often email people they do not know, so a small change in the address is easy to miss. This is about reading the sender address letter by letter, not the message text. A fake offer letter with an extra word in the address is a common trick. Always check that the address ends with synergymarinegroup.com. Confirm with the known HR crewing number before you share documents.

items.title: Real vs Fake Finance Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake Finance email uses the same payroll topic but adds fake urgency. It says "URGENT - Bank Detail Change - Action Required TODAY" and "miss this month's payment run". It also tells you not to follow the normal approval process and not to call back.
items.whyItsSuspicious: The real Finance notice is calm. It says "scheduled for the regular payment run on 28 Nov" and "no immediate action required". It says "call back on the known vendor number to check any bank detail change". For Finance, pressure to skip checks is the warning sign. Threats about deadlines, fear of missed pay, or orders to skip the normal process are the clue. Urgency that tells you to change bank details without a call back is the real warning. The address is not the issue here.

items.title: Real vs Fake Payslip Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake HR email has unexpected attachments. One is Payslip_March.pdf.exe, which ends with .exe. The other is a generic Documents.zip. It asks you to "Enable Content" or enter a password. The real payslip email has expected files with clear names: Payslip_Feb2025_RajKumar.pdf and Rotation_Roster_MV-Horizon_Feb-Apr.xlsx. They have the correct icons and sizes.
items.whyItsSuspicious: HR often sends payslips and rosters, so fake attachments blend in. Ask: did you expect this file? Does the name and type match the context? A payslip should be a PDF. A roster should be a spreadsheet. You should not need macros. Watch for double endings like .pdf.exe, generic ZIP files, or vague subjects like "Updated Payslip - Please Review Immediately". Check with HR on a known channel before you open it.

items.title: Real vs Fake Rotation Email
items.whatIsWrong: Both rotation emails show the same link text: portal.synergymarinegroup.com. But the fake email goes to a different place. If you hover, it shows https://portal-synergymarine-group-secure.net/crew/verify?id=42 and a short link http://bit.ly/CrewRotation-Horizon. The real email link truly goes to portal.synergymarinegroup.com. Both are addressed to offshore crew, Rajesh Kumar, 3rd Officer, MV Horizon.
items.whyItsSuspicious: When you are offshore with limited time and internet, a quick tap is tempting. This is about where the link goes, not who sent it. Always press and hold or hover to check the real address. Look for the exact domain portal.synergymarinegroup.com. Do not trust short links or links with extra hyphens. Use a bookmarked portal or check with your vessel manager when you are back online.

items.title: Real vs Fake Crew Portal
items.whatIsWrong: The fake crew portal address is "portal.synergymanne-group.com" with an extra "n". The real address is "portal.synergymarinegroup.com". The login screens otherwise look exactly the same.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Attackers can copy the look of the crew portal exactly. But they cannot fake the real address. Always check the address bar before you enter your login details. When you can, use a bookmarked link. This is the same habit as checking links in emails.

items.title: Scam Text Message
items.whatIsWrong: A text message pretends to be from a delivery service. It asks you to check a package using an unfamiliar link.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Real delivery companies rarely send you a link to check a package out of the blue. The short, fake-looking link and pressure to act now are signs of smishing. Smishing is phishing by text. It can target staff on shore or crew during travel.

items.title: Fake IT Pop-Up
items.whatIsWrong: A pop-up that claims to be from IT support asks you to type your password into the box to fix an error.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Real IT will never ask for your password in a pop-up. This is true on shore and offshore. This is a trick to steal your login. It is dressed up as a normal system message. It can target any role.

items.title: MFA Prompt Flood
items.whatIsWrong: You get many MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication - the extra approval step after your password) requests that you did not ask for. The attacker hopes you will tap Approve just to make them stop.
items.whyItsSuspicious: One unexpected MFA request is worth noticing. Many requests in a few minutes means someone already has your password. They are trying to wear you down until you approve by mistake. This can happen on shore or offshore.
